hints: Measure the long filamentous virus from head to tail tip on the printed image with a ruler in millimetres. It should be about 60 to 70 mm long.
Remember actual size = image size divided by magnification, then convert your mm measurement into nm using 1 mm = 1,000,000 nm.
walkthrough:
**Measure the image size**

Grab a ruler and measure the full length of the virus in the micrograph from the round head to the tip of the tail.

You should get about $66 \text{ mm}$ (your exact value may vary slightly with printing, around 60 to 70 mm is fine).

**Apply the magnification formula**

Magnification tells us how many times bigger the image is than the real object.

Use:
$$\text{actual size} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}}$$
$$\text{actual size} = \frac{66 \text{ mm}}{60\,000} = 0.0011 \text{ mm}$$

**Convert mm to nm and choose**

Viruses are tiny, so we express the answer in nanometres. Remember $1 \text{ mm} = 1,000,000 \text{ nm}$.

So:
$$0.0011 \text{ mm} \times 1,000,000 = 1100 \text{ nm}$$
This matches option D, which is a sensible size for a large filamentous virus.

options.A: Too small by a factor of 1000. This would come from a unit conversion error, such as confusing micrometres and nanometres.
options.B: Too small by a factor of 100. This is far smaller than any virus and suggests dividing by too large a magnification or misplacing decimals.
options.C: Too small by a factor of 10. This is a common slip when converting mm to nm or when the image length is mismeasured.
options.D: Correct. An image of about 66 mm divided by 60,000 gives 0.0011 mm, which equals 1100 nm.
